overview.title: Chapter 11 opener: Image segmentation
overview.main_topic: Opening page of chapter 11: what the chapter covers (the branches of computer vision, a segmentation model built from scratch, and the pretrained Segment Anything Model) and the start of section 11.1 on the main computer vision tasks.
overview.central_idea: Image classification (one image in, one label out) is only one computer vision task. This chapter moves to image segmentation, after first placing it among the three essential tasks: classification, segmentation, and object detection.
overview.importance: It marks the shift from image-level predictions (chapters 8-10) to pixel-level predictions. Segmentation brings new output formats (masks), new architectures (downsampling followed by upsampling), and the use of a large pretrained foundation model.
learning_objectives: Know the three topics the chapter promises to cover.
See image classification as one of several computer vision tasks.
Prepare to distinguish classification, segmentation, and detection (listed on p.333).
prerequisites: Binary image classification with ConvNets (chapter 8, from p.255)

summary:
This is the opening page of **chapter 11, Image segmentation**. The "This chapter covers" box lists three topics:

- the different branches of computer vision: **image classification, image segmentation, and object detection**;
- **building a segmentation model from scratch** (section 11.2, from p.335);
- **using the pretrained Segment Anything Model** (section 11.3, from p.342).

The introduction recalls that chapter 8 introduced deep learning for vision through a simple use case, *binary image classification*, and says computer vision is more than that. This chapter goes deeper into another essential application, image segmentation.

Section **11.1 Computer vision tasks** begins by summarizing what classification does: "an image goes in, a label comes out" ("this image likely contains a cat; this other one likely contains a dog"). It then states that there are three essential computer vision tasks to know about. The list itself (classification, segmentation, detection, with figure 11.1) continues on p.333.

**How to use this page:** treat it as a roadmap. The chapter first sets out the task landscape and the types of segmentation (semantic, instance, panoptic; p.334), then trains a small segmentation model on a downloaded dataset, and finally shows how to prompt SAM with points and boxes. Object detection, mentioned in the first bullet, is covered in detail in chapter 12 (p.334, p.354).

paragraphs.excerpt: Chapter 8 gave you a first introduction to deep learning for
paragraphs.what_it_says: Chapter 8 introduced deep learning for computer vision through binary image classification, but computer vision is more than classification. This chapter goes deeper into another essential application, image segmentation.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The skills from chapter 8 (ConvNets, data pipelines, pretrained models) now get applied to a task with a richer output: a label for every pixel instead of one label per image.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It sets the scope of the chapter and connects it to what the reader already knows.

terminology.meaning: Partitioning an image into regions, usually by assigning a class to each pixel (defined on pp.333-334).

connections: p.255: chapter 8 opener (ConvNets, data augmentation, feature extraction, fine-tuning).
p.334: segmentation can be approached 'straightforwardly' with what has been learned so far.

paragraphs.excerpt: So far, we’ve focused on image classification models: an image goes
paragraphs.what_it_says: So far the book has covered image classification: an image goes in and a label comes out ('this image likely contains a cat; this other one likely contains a dog'). That is only one possible application, and there are three essential computer vision tasks to know about.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The tasks differ in the structure of their output: one label (or a set of labels) for the whole image, a label per pixel, or a set of labeled boxes.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Choosing the right task formulation comes first in any vision project. The book returns to this choice when it compares segmentation and detection costs (p.354).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: output shapes make the difference concrete. Classification gives (num_classes,), semantic segmentation gives (H, W, num_classes), and detection gives a variable-length list of (box, class) pairs.

terminology.meaning: Assigning one or more labels to a whole image.

connections: p.333: the three tasks (classification, segmentation, object detection) and figure 11.1.
p.354: segmentation is a strict superset of detection but costs more to run and to label.

concepts.name: The three essential computer vision tasks
concepts.definition: Image classification, image segmentation, and object detection, which the book says nearly all vision applications reduce to (p.334).
concepts.intuition: What is in the picture? Which pixels belong to what? Where are the objects, roughly?
concepts.technical: The tasks differ in output granularity: image-level labels, pixel-level masks, and box-level labels.
concepts.example: Photo search (classification), video-call background replacement (segmentation), and self-driving perception (detection), all examples given on p.333.
concepts.misconception: That classification is all of computer vision.

questions.question: What three topics does chapter 11 say it covers?
questions.answer: The branches of computer vision (image classification, image segmentation, object detection), building a segmentation model from scratch, and using the pretrained Segment Anything Model.

questions.question: How does the book summarize what an image classification model does?
options: An image goes in, a label comes out
An image goes in, a mask the size of the image comes out
An image goes in, a list of bounding boxes comes out
A label goes in, an image comes out
questions.answer: An image goes in, a label comes out
questions.explanation: Quoted from p332_e11. A mask is the output of segmentation, boxes are the output of detection, and label-to-image is generation (chapter 17).

questions.question: Which use case did chapter 8 use to introduce deep learning for computer vision?
questions.explanation: p332_e09 says 'binary image classification'. The dogs-vs-cats dataset is the chapter 8 example.

questions.question: Why might the authors begin a segmentation chapter by surveying several vision tasks rather than going straight to segmentation?
questions.answer: Comparing tasks by what they output (a label, a per-pixel mask, labeled boxes) shows what is new about segmentation and helps you choose the right formulation for a problem. For example, detection is cheaper when pixel precision is not needed (p.354).
questions.explanation: This is an interpretation of the chapter structure. The page itself only states that classification is one of three essential tasks.

questions.question: Before turning the page, can you guess what the outputs of segmentation and object detection look like, compared with classification?
questions.answer: Self-check: segmentation outputs a class for every pixel (a mask the size of the image), and detection outputs bounding boxes, each with a class. Compare with p.333.
